cover.title: Matthew
cover.subtitle: The Gospel, Its World and Your Notes

intro.author: Matthew the apostle (by tradition)
paras: The Gospel does not name its author, but the early church unanimously credited it to Matthew, also called Levi, the tax collector Jesus called to follow Him (9:9; 10:3). Around AD 125 Papias wrote that Matthew recorded Jesus’ sayings in the Hebrew (Aramaic) language. Writing mainly for Jewish believers, Matthew shows again and again that Jesus fulfills the Scriptures. Where he wrote is uncertain; Antioch of Syria is the most common suggestion.
intro.note: Because the book is anonymous, its authorship rests on church tradition. Many modern scholars date it to AD 80–90 and doubt an apostle wrote it; this study follows the traditional view.
facts: About 2 hours 20 minutes, or a few sittings

learn.title: The promised King
learn.text: How Jesus’ family line, birth and early years fulfill the Scriptures and show Him to be the son of David and of Abraham.

learn.title: The Sermon on the Mount
learn.text: What life in the kingdom looks like: true blessing, inner righteousness, prayer, trust in the Father and building on Jesus’ words.

learn.title: Parables of the kingdom
learn.text: How the kingdom grows quietly like seed, leaven and hidden treasure, and why some hear while others do not.

learn.title: Who is Jesus?
learn.text: Peter confesses Jesus as the Christ, the Son of God, and Jesus gives His first plain warning of the cross.

learn.title: Life together
learn.text: How Jesus’ followers should treat the humble, seek the straying, correct a brother who sins and forgive without limit.

learn.title: Cross, empty tomb, commission
learn.text: How the King is crucified, rises from the dead and sends His disciples to make disciples of all the nations.

shape.label: Chapters 1–16
shape.title: Who is the King?
shape.text: Birth, teaching and miracles in Galilee, leading up to Peter’s confession at 16:16.

shape.label: Chapters 16–25
shape.title: The road to the cross
shape.text: From 16:21 Jesus speaks plainly of His death and heads for Jerusalem.

shape.label: Chapters 26–28
shape.title: Death and resurrection
shape.text: The Last Supper, the cross, the empty tomb and the Great Commission.

intro.turning: The turning point: “And Simon Peter answered and said, Thou art the Christ, the Son of the living God.” (16:16)

keyverse.text: “Go ye therefore, and make disciples of all the nations, baptizing them into the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit:”

intro.asread: Watch for the phrase “kingdom of heaven”. Matthew uses it over thirty times, and no other New Testament

cover.title: Mark
cover.subtitle: The Gospel, Its World and Your Notes
meta: Written about AD 65–70, likely in Rome

intro.author: John Mark (by tradition)
paras: Mark does not name its author, but early church writers agree it was John Mark, whose mother’s home in Jerusalem was a meeting place for the church (Acts 12:12). He traveled with Paul and Barnabas and later worked with Peter (1 Pet 5:13). Around AD 125 Papias wrote that Mark was Peter’s interpreter, who wrote down what Peter remembered. He most likely wrote in Rome, for Gentile believers facing Nero’s persecution.
intro.note: The book is anonymous, so its authorship rests on early tradition, which many scholars still accept. Some date it a little earlier, in the late 50s; this study follows the traditional view.
facts: About 1 hour 25 minutes, or a few sittings

learn.title: The kingdom at hand
learn.text: How Jesus is baptized, tested in the wilderness and begins preaching, calling fishermen to follow Him.

learn.title: Authority over all
learn.text: Jesus’ power over demons, disease, sin, storm and death, and the growing opposition it stirs up.

learn.title: Who do you say?
learn.text: Peter confesses Jesus as the Christ, and Jesus begins to teach that the Son of man must suffer.

learn.title: The way of the servant
learn.text: Three times Jesus foretells His death, and each time He teaches that true greatness means serving others.

learn.title: The final week
learn.text: Jesus enters Jerusalem, clears the temple, answers His opponents and warns that the temple will fall.

learn.title: Cross and empty tomb
learn.text: Jesus is betrayed, tried and crucified, a Roman centurion confesses Him, and the tomb is found empty.

shape.label: Chapters 1–8
shape.title: Who is Jesus?
shape.text: Miracles and teaching in Galilee lead up to Peter’s confession at 8:29.

shape.label: Chapters 8–10
shape.title: The way to the cross
shape.text: On the road, Jesus three times foretells His death and teaches servanthood.

shape.label: Chapters 11–16
shape.title: The final week
shape.text: Jerusalem, the cross and the empty tomb fill more than a third of the book.

intro.turning: The turning point: “And he asked them, But who say ye that I am? Peter answereth and saith unto him, Thou art the Christ.” (8:29)

keyverse.text: “For the Son of man also came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ransom for many.”

intro.asread: Watch for the word “straightway”. Mark uses it over forty times, moving quickly from scene to scene, and

cover.title: Luke
cover.subtitle: The Gospel, Its World and Your Notes

intro.author: Luke the physician (by tradition)
paras: Luke does not name himself, but early church writers agree that Luke wrote this Gospel and its sequel, Acts. Paul calls him “the beloved physician” (Col 4:14), and the “we” passages in Acts show the author traveling with Paul. Not an eyewitness himself, Luke carefully gathered accounts from those who were (1:1–4) and wrote for Theophilus, likely a man of rank, probably around AD 60–62.
intro.note: The book is anonymous, but Luke’s authorship is widely held. Many scholars date it to AD 80–90 rather than about AD 60–62; this study follows the traditional view.
facts: Theophilus, and Gentile readers like him
About 2 hours 30 minutes, or a few sittings

learn.title: Births foretold and fulfilled
learn.text: Why Luke wrote, and how angels announce the births of John the Baptist and of Jesus, the promised Savior.

learn.title: Good news for the poor
learn.text: Jesus announces His mission at Nazareth and begins healing, calling disciples and welcoming sinners to His table.

learn.title: The road to Jerusalem
learn.text: Jesus sets out for Jerusalem, sending out the seventy and teaching about prayer, discipleship and money.

learn.title: Lost and found
learn.text: Three parables of a lost sheep, a lost coin and a lost son show God’s joy over one sinner who repents.

learn.title: The innocent Savior
learn.text: Pilate declares Jesus innocent three times, yet He is crucified and promises paradise to a dying criminal.

learn.title: He is risen
learn.text: The empty tomb, the walk to Emmaus and Jesus opening the Scriptures to show He had to suffer and rise.

shape.label: Chapters 1–9
shape.title: Ministry in Galilee
shape.text: Births, baptism and ministry in Galilee, until Jesus sets out for Jerusalem at 9:51.

shape.label: Chapters 9–19
shape.title: The journey to Jerusalem
shape.text: Teaching and parables on the road, much of it found only in Luke.

shape.label: Chapters 19–24
shape.title: Cross and resurrection
shape.text: Jesus enters Jerusalem, dies, rises and is carried up into heaven near Bethany.

intro.turning: The turning point: “And it came to pass, when the days were well-nigh come that he should be received up, he stedfastly set his face to go to Jerusalem,” (9:51)

keyverse.text: “For the Son of man came to seek and to save that which was lost.”

intro.asread: Watch for people on the edges: women, the poor, Samaritans, tax collectors and sinners. Luke keeps showing Jesus welcoming them, and heaven rejoicing when the lost are found.

cover.title: John
cover.subtitle: The Gospel, Its World and Your Notes
meta: Written about AD 85–95, likely in Ephesus

intro.author: John the apostle (by tradition)
paras: The Gospel never names its writer, calling him only “the disciple whom Jesus loved,” who saw these things and wrote them down (21:20–24). Early church tradition identifies him as John the apostle, son of Zebedee. Irenaeus, who knew John’s disciple Polycarp, wrote around AD 180 that John published the Gospel while living in Ephesus. It was probably the last Gospel written, late in John’s long life.
intro.note: Some scholars think a circle of John’s followers shaped the final book from his witness; this study follows the traditional view that John himself wrote it.
facts: Believers and seekers, Jewish and Gentile
About 1 hour 50 minutes, or a few sittings

learn.title: The Word made flesh
learn.text: Who Jesus was before time began, and how the eternal Word became a man and made the Father known.

learn.title: Signs that reveal Him
learn.text: Water into wine, healings and the feeding of five thousand: miracles that show Jesus’ glory and call for faith.

learn.title: Born anew
learn.text: Why even a teacher like Nicodemus must be born of the Spirit, and how God so loved the world.

learn.title: The “I am” sayings
learn.text: Jesus calls Himself the bread of life, the light of the world, the good shepherd, and the resurrection and the life.

learn.title: The upper room
learn.text: Jesus washes His disciples’ feet, promises the Holy Spirit and prays for all who will believe in Him.

learn.title: Death and new life
learn.text: Jesus is crucified and rises, then meets Mary and Thomas and restores Peter beside the sea.

shape.label: Chapters 1–12
shape.title: The book of signs
shape.text: Jesus shows His glory through signs and sayings, yet many refuse to believe.

shape.label: Chapters 13–21
shape.title: The book of glory
shape.text: His hour has come: He prepares His disciples, dies, rises and sends them out.

intro.turning: The turning point: “And Jesus answereth them, saying, The hour is come, that the Son of man should be glorified.” (12:23)

keyverse.text: “but these are written, that ye may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God; and that believing ye may have life in his name.”

intro.asread: Watch for the word “believe”. John uses it nearly a hundred times, yet never the noun faith. He wants readers to keep trusting Jesus, not just hold an idea about Him.

cover.eyebrow: A Study Of The Acts Of The
cover.title: Acts
cover.subtitle: The History, Its World and Your Notes

intro.author: Luke the physician (by tradition)
paras: Acts does not name its author, but it continues the Gospel of Luke and is addressed to the same Theophilus (1:1). Early church writers agree it was Luke, the physician and Paul’s companion, and in the “we” passages (16:10–17; 20:5–21:18; 27:1–28:16) the writer was there himself. Acts ends with Paul under house arrest in Rome, still awaiting trial, so Luke most likely finished it there around AD 62.
intro.note: Luke’s authorship is widely accepted. Many scholars date Acts to the AD 80s rather than about AD 62; this study follows the earlier, traditional date.
facts: About 2 hours 20 minutes, or a few sittings

learn.title: The Spirit comes
learn.text: Jesus ascends, the Holy Spirit is poured out at Pentecost, Peter preaches and about three thousand believe.

learn.title: The church in Jerusalem
learn.text: How the first believers shared their lives, prayed, faced threats and kept speaking boldly about Jesus.

learn.title: Stephen and the scattering
learn.text: Stephen is martyred, the believers are scattered, and the gospel reaches Samaria and an Ethiopian official.

learn.title: Saul and Cornelius
learn.text: The persecutor Saul meets the risen Jesus, and Peter learns that God accepts Gentiles too.

learn.title: Paul’s journeys
learn.text: Paul and his companions preach in Cyprus, plant churches in Galatia, Macedonia, Greece and Asia, and the Jerusalem council welcomes Gentiles.

learn.title: Prisoner bound for Rome
learn.text: Paul is arrested, defends himself before rulers, survives a shipwreck and preaches in Rome under house arrest.

shape.label: Chapters 1–7
shape.title: Witness in Jerusalem
shape.text: The Spirit comes and the church grows in the city, until Stephen’s death.

shape.label: Chapters 8–12
shape.title: Judea and Samaria
shape.text: Scattered believers spread the word; Saul is converted; Gentiles believe.

shape.label: Chapters 13–28
shape.title: To the uttermost part
shape.text: Paul carries the gospel west across the empire, ending in Rome.

intro.turning: The turning point: “And as they ministered to the Lord, and fasted, the Holy Spirit said, Separate me Barnabas and Saul for the work whereunto I have called them.” (13:2)

keyverse.text: “But ye shall receive power, when the Holy Spirit is come upon you: and ye shall be my witnesses both in Jerusalem, and in all Judæa and Samaria, and unto the uttermost part of the earth.”

intro.asread: Watch for the Holy Spirit. He is named more than forty times in Acts, and at each new step, from

cover.title: Romans
cover.subtitle: The Letter, Its World and Your Notes
meta: Sent to the church in Rome under Nero

intro.author: Paul the apostle
paras: Paul names himself at the start (1:1), and his scribe Tertius adds his own greeting near the end (16:22). Paul had never visited Rome, though he knew many believers there by name (16:3–15). He wrote from Corinth about AD 57, near the end of his third journey, just before taking the collection to Jerusalem (15:25), and hoped to visit Rome on his way to Spain (15:24).
facts: Corinth, near the end of Paul’s third journey
The believers in Rome, Jews and Gentiles

learn.title: All have sinned
learn.text: Why Gentiles and Jews alike stand guilty before God, and why no one is made right by keeping the law.

learn.title: Righteous by faith
learn.text: How God justifies the ungodly as a free gift received through faith in Christ, just as he counted Abraham righteous.

learn.title: Grace that reigns
learn.text: What Adam’s sin and Christ’s obedience mean for us, and why grace frees us from sin’s rule rather than excusing it.

learn.title: Life in the Spirit
learn.text: Why there is no condemnation in Christ, how the Spirit gives life and hope, and why nothing can separate us from God’s love.

learn.title: God and Israel
learn.text: How God’s promises to Israel still stand, why many Jews had not believed, and how his mercy reaches Jew and Gentile.

learn.title: Living sacrifices
learn.text: How the gospel reshapes worship, love, life under rulers, and how strong and weak believers should welcome one another.

shape.label: Chapters 1–8
shape.title: The gospel explained
shape.text: Sin, justification by faith, new life and the Spirit’s work in believers.

shape.label: Chapters 9–11
shape.title: God’s faithfulness to Israel
shape.text: How God’s plan for Israel and the nations holds together.

shape.label: Chapters 12–16
shape.title: The gospel lived
shape.text: Commands for daily life and church unity, then Paul’s plans and greetings. The turn comes at 12:1.

intro.turning: The turning point: “I beseech you therefore, brethren, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable to God, which is your spiritual service.” (12:1)

keyverse.text: “For I am not ashamed of the gospel: for it is the power of God unto salvation to every one that believeth; to the Jew first, and also to the Greek.”

intro.asread: Watch for the phrase “a righteousness of God” (1:17; 3:21). Paul shows that God is both right and the one who makes sinners right with himself through faith.

cover.title: 1 Corinthians
cover.subtitle: The Letter, Its World and Your Notes
meta: Sent to the church in Corinth

intro.author: Paul the apostle
paras: Paul names himself, writing with Sosthenes (1:1). He had founded the church in Corinth about AD 50–52 and stayed eighteen months (Acts 18). He wrote from Ephesus (16:8) about AD 54–55, answering reports from “the household of Chloe” (1:11) and a letter of questions from the church (7:1). He mentions an earlier letter (5:9) that has not survived.
facts: Ephesus, during Paul’s long stay there
The church in Corinth, which Paul had founded

learn.title: Divisions and the cross
learn.text: Why rival loyalties to leaders miss the point, and how the cross overturns the world’s ideas of wisdom and power.

learn.title: A holy church
learn.text: How to deal with open sin, lawsuits between believers and sexual immorality, since the body is a temple of the Spirit.

learn.title: Marriage and singleness
learn.text: Paul’s answers about marriage, divorce and remaining single, and how to serve the Lord in whatever state we are called.

learn.title: Freedom limited by love
learn.text: What to do about food offered to idols, and why love gives up rights so that others do not stumble.

learn.title: Worship and gifts
learn.text: Order in worship, the Lord’s Supper, many gifts in one body, and why love matters more than any gift.

learn.title: The resurrection
learn.text: Why Christ’s rising is at the heart of the gospel, and what it promises for the bodies of those who belong to him.

shape.label: Chapters 1–6
shape.title: Problems reported to Paul
shape.text: Divisions, immorality and lawsuits that Paul had heard about from others.

shape.label: Chapters 7–16
shape.title: Answers to their questions
shape.text: Marriage, idol food, worship, the resurrection and the collection, often introduced by “now concerning.”

intro.turning: The turning point: “Now concerning the things whereof ye wrote: It is good for a man not to touch a woman.” (7:1)

keyverse.text: “For the word of the cross is to them that perish foolishness; but unto us who are saved it is the power of God.”

intro.asread: Watch for “now concerning” (7:1; 8:1; 12:1; 16:1). Each one opens a new question from the church’s letter, and shows Paul bringing the cross to bear on everyday church problems.

cover.title: 2 Corinthians
cover.subtitle: The Letter, Its World and Your Notes
meta: Sent to the church in Corinth

intro.author: Paul the apostle
paras: Paul names himself, writing with Timothy (1:1). After 1 Corinthians he made a painful visit to the church (2:1) and sent a tearful letter (2:4). Waiting anxiously in Macedonia, he met Titus, who brought news that the church had repented (7:5–7). Paul then wrote this letter from Macedonia, perhaps Philippi, about AD 55–56, perhaps the most personal of all his letters.
intro.note: Paul’s authorship is not in doubt. Some scholars think the letter combines two or more of Paul’s letters, especially chapters 10–13; this study reads it as one letter.
facts: The church in Corinth and believers throughout Achaia

learn.title: Comfort in affliction
learn.text: How the God of all comfort meets us in our suffering so that we can comfort others in theirs.

learn.title: A painful visit
learn.text: Why Paul changed his travel plans, why he wrote with tears, and why the church should now forgive the offender.

learn.title: Treasure in earthen vessels
learn.text: How God’s glory shines through weak and suffering servants, and why believers do not lose heart.

learn.title: Reconciled to God
learn.text: How Christ’s death makes a new creation, and why God entrusts his people with the message of reconciliation.

learn.title: Cheerful giving
learn.text: What the generous Macedonians and Christ’s own poverty teach about giving freely and gladly to help other believers.

learn.title: Strength in weakness
learn.text: Paul’s defense against rival teachers, his boasting in weakness, his thorn in the flesh, and grace that is enough.

shape.label: Chapters 1–7
shape.title: Paul’s ministry explained
shape.text: Comfort, forgiveness, the new covenant and reconciliation, told through Paul’s own trials.

shape.label: Chapters 8–9
shape.title: The collection
shape.text: An appeal to finish their gift for the poor believers in Jerusalem.

shape.label: Chapters 10–13
shape.title: Paul’s defense
shape.text: A sharp reply to rivals who despised his weakness. The tone changes at 10:1.

intro.turning: The turning point: “Now I Paul myself entreat you by the meekness and gentleness of Christ, I who in your presence am lowly among you, but being absent am of good courage toward you:” (10:1)

keyverse.text: “Wherefore if any man is in Christ, he is a new creature: the old things are passed away; behold, they are become new.”

intro.asread: Watch for the words “comfort” and “weakness”. Paul keeps pointing to what makes him look weak, because that is where God’s comfort and power are seen most clearly.

cover.title: Galatians
cover.subtitle: The Letter, Its World and Your Notes
meta: Sent to the churches of Galatia

intro.author: Paul the apostle
paras: Paul names himself (1:1) and writes the closing lines in his own hand, with “large letters” (6:11). He had first preached in Galatia during an illness, and the believers welcomed him warmly (4:13–15). When teachers later told them to be circumcised and keep the Law, he wrote sharply, probably from Antioch of Syria about AD 48–49.
intro.note: Paul’s authorship is not in doubt. Scholars debate whether “Galatia” means the southern cities of his first journey or the north, and whether he wrote before the Jerusalem council or in the 50s; this study follows the early date.
facts: The churches of Galatia, likely those of Paul’s first journey

learn.title: No other gospel
learn.text: Why Paul is astonished that they are turning away so quickly, and why any message other than grace must be rejected.

learn.title: Paul’s own story
learn.text: How Paul received his gospel from Christ, was accepted by the Jerusalem leaders, and confronted Peter at Antioch.

learn.title: Justified by faith
learn.text: Why Abraham was counted righteous by faith, what the Law was for, and how believers become sons and heirs.

learn.title: Slavery or freedom
learn.text: Paul’s personal plea to the Galatians and his picture of Hagar and Sarah as two covenants of slavery and freedom.

learn.title: Walking by the Spirit
learn.text: How freedom is not a license for the flesh, what the fruit of the Spirit is, and how to bear one another’s burdens.

shape.label: Chapters 1–2
shape.title: The gospel defended
shape.text: Paul’s story shows his gospel came from Christ, not from any man.

shape.label: Chapters 3–4
shape.title: The gospel explained
shape.text: Scripture shows that people are made right with God by faith, not law.

shape.label: Chapters 5–6
shape.title: The gospel lived
shape.text: Freedom in Christ, walking by the Spirit and caring for one another.

intro.turning: The turning point: “For freedom did Christ set us free: stand fast therefore, and be not entangled again in a yoke of bondage.” (5:1)

keyverse.text: “Now that no man is justified by the law before God, is evident: for, The righteous shall live by faith;”

intro.asread: Watch the pairs Paul sets side by side: law and promise, slavery and freedom, flesh and Spirit. Each pair

cover.title: Ephesians
cover.subtitle: The Letter, Its World and Your Notes

intro.author: Paul the apostle
paras: Paul names himself at the start (1:1) and calls himself “the prisoner of Christ Jesus” (3:1). He knew the Ephesian believers well: he spent nearly three years in their city (Acts 19–20), longer than anywhere else on his journeys. He wrote this letter from prison, most likely in Rome, and sent it with Tychicus along with Colossians and Philemon.
intro.note: The church has received Ephesians as Paul’s from the earliest times. Some modern scholars think a close follower wrote it in his name; this study follows the traditional view.
facts: The believers at Ephesus, and likely the churches around it

learn.title: Every spiritual blessing
learn.text: What God has already given those who are in Christ: chosen, adopted, forgiven and sealed by the Holy Spirit.

learn.title: Saved by grace
learn.text: Why salvation is God’s gift received through faith, not something earned, and what good works are for.

learn.title: One new people
learn.text: How Christ broke down the wall between Jew and Gentile and made one family, one body, one holy temple.

learn.title: Walking worthy
learn.text: What unity looks like in a church, why God gives different gifts, and how believers grow up into Christ.

learn.title: A changed life at home
learn.text: How the gospel reshapes speech, habits, marriage, parents and children, and work.

learn.title: The armor of God
learn.text: How to stand firm in the spiritual battle with truth, righteousness, faith, the word of God and prayer.

shape.label: Chapters 1–3
shape.title: What God has done
shape.text: Blessings, grace and one new people in Christ. Almost no commands.

shape.label: Chapters 4–6
shape.title: How then to live
shape.text: Unity, holiness, home and spiritual battle. Paul turns to commands at 4:1.

intro.turning: The turning point: “I therefore, the prisoner in the Lord, beseech you to walk worthily of the calling wherewith ye were called,” (4:1)

keyverse.text: “for by grace have ye been saved through faith; and that not of yourselves, it is the gift of God;”

intro.asread: Watch for the small words “in Christ” and “in him”. They appear again and again in chapter 1 alone and carry the heart of the letter.

cover.title: Philippians
cover.subtitle: The Letter, Its World and Your Notes
meta: Written about AD 60–62 from prison in Rome
Sent to the church at Philippi

intro.author: Paul the apostle
paras: Paul names himself, writing with Timothy (1:1). He founded the church at Philippi on his second journey, his first church in Europe (Acts 16), and the believers there supported him again and again (4:15–16). He wrote from prison, most likely in Rome, about AD 60–62, to thank them for a gift Epaphroditus had brought (4:18).
intro.note: Paul’s authorship is accepted by virtually all scholars. Some place the letter in an earlier imprisonment at Ephesus, about AD 54–55; this study follows the traditional Roman setting.
facts: The church at Philippi, with its bishops and deacons

learn.title: Joy in chains
learn.text: How Paul’s imprisonment actually advanced the gospel, and why for him to live is Christ and to die is gain.

learn.title: The mind of Christ
learn.text: How Christ humbled himself to the cross and was highly exalted, and why that pattern shapes how we treat one another.

learn.title: Shining as lights
learn.text: Why believers work out their salvation as God works in them, with Timothy and Epaphroditus as living examples.

learn.title: Knowing Christ
learn.text: Why Paul counted his impressive religious record as loss, and how he presses on toward the prize in Christ.

learn.title: Peace and contentment
learn.text: How to rejoice, pray instead of worrying, think on what is good, and learn contentment in every circumstance.

shape.label: Chapters 1–2
shape.title: Living worthy of the gospel
shape.text: Paul’s circumstances, and a call to unity modeled on Christ’s humility.

shape.label: Chapter 3
shape.title: Pressing on
shape.text: A warning against trusting the flesh, and Paul’s own race toward Christ.

shape.label: Chapter 4
shape.title: Joy and peace
shape.text: Agreement, prayer, contentment and thanks for the church’s generous gift.

keyverse.text: “For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain.”

intro.asread: Watch for “joy” and “rejoice”, about sixteen times in four short chapters. They come from a man in chains who did not know whether he would live or die.

cover.title: Colossians
cover.subtitle: The Letter, Its World and Your Notes
meta: Written about AD 60–62 from prison in Rome
Sent to the church at Colossae

intro.author: Paul the apostle
paras: Paul names himself, writing with Timothy (1:1), and signs the closing greeting “with mine own hand” (4:18). He had never visited Colossae; Epaphras, a Colossian, had brought them the gospel (1:7; 4:12). Paul wrote from prison, most likely in Rome, about AD 60–62, and sent the letter with Tychicus and Onesimus (4:7–9), along with Ephesians and Philemon.
intro.note: The early church received Colossians as Paul’s. Some modern scholars think a close follower wrote it in his name, pointing to its style and its close links with Ephesians; this study follows the traditional view.
facts: The believers at Colossae, a church Paul had not visited

learn.title: Thanks and prayer
learn.text: Why Paul thanks God for their faith and love, and prays that they will walk worthily and bear fruit.

learn.title: Christ above all
learn.text: Who Christ is: the image of the invisible God, maker of all things, head of the church, reconciling all through his cross.

learn.title: Complete in him
learn.text: Why believers need no added rules, rituals or worship of angels, since all the fullness of God dwells in Christ.

learn.title: Raised with Christ
learn.text: How to set the mind on things above, put off the old ways, and put on compassion, forgiveness, love and peace.

learn.title: Christ in the home
learn.text: How the Lord shapes wives and husbands, children and parents, servants and masters, and how believers pray and speak.

shape.label: Chapters 1–2
shape.title: Who Christ is
shape.text: Christ supreme over creation and the church, and all believers need.

shape.label: Chapters 3–4
shape.title: Living in Christ
shape.text: A raised life at home and in the world. Paul turns to commands at 3:1.

intro.turning: The turning point: “If then ye were raised together with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated on the right hand of God.” (3:1)

keyverse.text: “And he is the head of the body, the church: who is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead; that in all things he might have the preeminence.”

intro.asread: Watch for the little word “all”. Christ made all things, holds all things together, has the preeminence in all things, and in the end Christ is “all, and in all” (3:11).

cover.title: 1 Thessalonians
cover.subtitle: The Letter, Its World and Your Notes
meta: Sent to the church at Thessalonica

intro.author: Paul the apostle
paras: Paul writes with Silvanus (Silas) and Timothy (1:1). He founded the church on his second journey but had to leave after a short stay, when a mob rose against him (Acts 17:1–10). Anxious for them, he sent Timothy back. When Timothy returned to him in Corinth with good news (3:6), Paul wrote this letter, about AD 50–51.
facts: The young church at Thessalonica, mostly Gentile

learn.title: A model church
learn.text: How the Thessalonians turned from idols to serve the living God and to wait for his Son from heaven.

learn.title: Paul’s example
learn.text: How Paul and his companions lived among them, gentle as a nurse and working night and day so as not to burden them.

learn.title: Longing to see them
learn.text: Why Paul sent Timothy back, his joy at the good report, and his prayer that their love would abound.

learn.title: Living to please God
learn.text: What God’s will means for sexual purity, brotherly love, and a quiet life of working with one’s own hands.

learn.title: Hope at Christ’s coming
learn.text: What happens to believers who have died, and how to stay awake and ready for the day of the Lord.

shape.label: Chapters 1–3
shape.title: Thanks and remembrance
shape.text: Paul’s joy over their faith and his story of their time together.

shape.label: Chapters 4–5
shape.title: Holy living and hope
shape.text: Instructions for daily life and comfort about Christ’s return. The turn comes at 4:1.

intro.turning: The turning point: “Finally then, brethren, we beseech and exhort you in the Lord Jesus, that, as ye received of us how ye ought to walk and to please God, even as ye do walk,—that ye abound more and more.” (4:1)

keyverse.text: “For if we believe that Jesus died and rose again, even so them also that are fallen asleep in Jesus will God bring with him.”

intro.asread: Watch how each chapter ends by looking ahead to the Lord’s coming (1:10; 2:19; 3:13; 4:16–17; 5:23). The hope of his return runs through the whole letter.

cover.title: 2 Thessalonians
cover.subtitle: The Letter, Its World and Your Notes
meta: Sent to the church at Thessalonica

intro.author: Paul the apostle
paras: Paul writes again with Silvanus and Timothy (1:1) and signs the closing greeting in his own hand, “the token in every epistle” (3:17). He wrote from Corinth about AD 51, a few months after 1 Thessalonians, when the church was still suffering persecution and was unsettled by claims that the day of the Lord had already come (2:2).
intro.note: The early church received this letter as Paul’s. Some modern scholars think a later follower wrote it in his name, because its tone differs from 1 Thessalonians; this study follows the traditional view.
facts: Corinth, a few months after 1 Thessalonians

learn.title: Hope under persecution
learn.text: How God sees his people’s suffering, will set things right when Jesus is revealed, and counts them worthy of his kingdom.

learn.title: Before the Lord’s day
learn.text: Why that day had not yet come, the man of sin who must first be revealed, and the Lord’s victory over him.

learn.title: Stand fast
learn.text: Thanks for God’s choosing, a call to hold to what Paul taught, and the comfort that the Lord is faithful.

learn.title: Work and discipline
learn.text: Why believers who refuse to work should be warned, and how Paul himself worked so as not to be a burden.

shape.label: Chapter 1
shape.title: Encouragement in suffering
shape.text: God will repay their persecutors and give rest to his afflicted people.

shape.label: Chapter 2
shape.title: Before the day comes
shape.text: Correcting confusion about the day of the Lord and urging them to stand firm.

shape.label: Chapter 3
shape.title: Work and order
shape.text: Prayer requests, then commands about idle believers and church discipline.

intro.turning: The turning point: “Now we beseech you, brethren, touching the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, and our gathering together unto him;” (2:1)

keyverse.text: “So then, brethren, stand fast, and hold the traditions which ye were taught, whether by word, or by epistle of ours.”

intro.asread: Watch for the word “disorderly” in chapter 3 (3:6, 7, 11). Right belief about Christ’s return leads to steady, ordinary faithfulness, not idle waiting.

cover.title: 1 Timothy
cover.subtitle: The Letter, Its World and Your Notes

intro.author: Paul the apostle
paras: The letter names Paul as author (1:1) and is written to Timothy, his “true child in faith” (1:2), who had traveled with him since Lystra (Acts 16:1–3). Paul had left Timothy at Ephesus to correct false teachers while he went on to Macedonia (1:3). By tradition he wrote about AD 62–64, after his release from his first Roman imprisonment.
intro.note: 1 and 2 Timothy and Titus are called the Pastoral Letters. Many modern scholars think a follower of Paul wrote them later, pointing to their vocabulary and church setting; this study follows the traditional view that Paul wrote them.
facts: Timothy, leading the church at Ephesus

learn.title: Guarding sound teaching
learn.text: How to answer false teachers, and why Paul, the chief of sinners, is living proof of Christ’s mercy.

learn.title: Prayer and worship
learn.text: Why the church prays for all men, including rulers, since God desires all to be saved through one mediator.

learn.title: Leaders in God’s house
learn.text: The character required of overseers and deacons, and the great mystery of godliness revealed in Christ.

learn.title: A good minister
learn.text: How Timothy should resist false self-denial, train himself in godliness and set an example though he was young.

learn.title: Caring for the household
learn.text: How the church honors widows and elders, deals with sin among leaders, and how servants treat their masters.

learn.title: Contentment and riches
learn.text: Why godliness with contentment is great gain, the danger of loving money, and how the rich should use their wealth.

shape.label: Chapters 1–3
shape.title: Order in God’s house
shape.text: False teaching, prayer and worship, and the qualities of church leaders.

shape.label: Chapters 4–6
shape.title: Timothy’s own ministry
shape.text: Personal charges to Timothy about teaching, caring for groups in the church, and money.

keyverse.text: “Faithful is the saying, and worthy of all acceptation, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners; of whom I am chief:”

intro.asread: Watch for “Faithful is the saying” (1:15; 3:1; 4:9). These short sayings seem to be well-known summaries of the faith that Paul wants Timothy to hold onto.

cover.title: 2 Timothy
cover.subtitle: The Letter, Its World and Your Notes
meta: Written about AD 66–67 from prison in Rome

intro.author: Paul the apostle
paras: The letter names Paul as author (1:1) and is written to Timothy, his “beloved child” (1:2), probably still at Ephesus. Paul is a prisoner in Rome again, in chains and hard to find (1:16–17), and he expects to die soon (4:6). By tradition this is his last letter, written about AD 66–67 under Nero, shortly before his execution.
intro.note: 1 and 2 Timothy and Titus are called the Pastoral Letters. Many modern scholars think a follower of Paul wrote them later, pointing to their vocabulary and church setting; this study follows the traditional view that Paul wrote them.

learn.title: Not ashamed
learn.text: Why Timothy should stir up his gift, not be ashamed of the gospel or of Paul, and guard what was entrusted to him.

learn.title: A good soldier
learn.text: How to pass the faith on to faithful men and endure hardship like a soldier, an athlete and a farmer.

learn.title: An approved workman
learn.text: How to handle the word of truth rightly, avoid foolish quarrels, flee youthful lusts and gently correct opponents.

learn.title: Hard times and Scripture
learn.text: What the last days will be like, why the godly will be persecuted, and why Scripture is enough to equip us.

learn.title: Finishing the race
learn.text: Paul’s charge to preach the word, his farewell as his life is poured out, and his last requests.

shape.label: Chapters 1–2
shape.title: Endure and pass it on
shape.text: Courage, faithfulness and handing the gospel on to the next generation.

shape.label: Chapters 3–4
shape.title: Hold to Scripture to the end
shape.text: Hard times ahead, the sufficiency of Scripture, and Paul’s farewell.

keyverse.text: “And the things which thou hast heard from me among many witnesses, the same commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also.”

intro.asread: Watch for “suffer hardship” (1:8; 2:3, 9; 4:5). Paul does not hide the cost of the gospel. He invites Timothy to share it, as he faces his own death.

cover.title: Titus
cover.subtitle: The Letter, Its World and Your Notes

intro.author: Paul the apostle
paras: The letter names Paul as author (1:1) and is written to Titus, his “true child after a common faith” (1:4), a Gentile co-worker (Gal 2:3) trusted with the troubled church at Corinth (2 Cor 7–8). Paul had left him on Crete to set things in order and appoint elders (1:5). By tradition he wrote about AD 63–65, between his two Roman imprisonments.
intro.note: 1 and 2 Timothy and Titus are called the Pastoral Letters. Many modern scholars think a follower of Paul wrote them later, pointing to their vocabulary and church setting; this study follows the traditional view that Paul wrote them.
facts: Titus, on the island of Crete

learn.title: Elders in every city
learn.text: The character and faithfulness Titus should look for in the leaders he appoints for the young churches.

learn.title: Silencing false teachers
learn.text: Why empty talkers who upset whole households must be corrected, and how their deeds deny the God they claim.

learn.title: Grace that trains us
learn.text: How older and younger believers and servants should live, because God’s grace teaches us to live godly lives.

learn.title: Saved to do good
learn.text: How believers live as good citizens, saved by God’s mercy and not by works, and ready for every good work.

shape.label: Chapter 1
shape.title: Leaders and false teachers
shape.text: Appointing faithful elders and silencing those who teach for gain.

shape.label: Chapter 2
shape.title: Sound living in the church
shape.text: What each group should do, grounded in the grace of God.

shape.label: Chapter 3
shape.title: Good works in the world
shape.text: How the saved should live among outsiders, and Paul’s final instructions.

keyverse.text: “For the grace of God hath appeared, bringing salvation to all men,”

intro.asread: Watch for “good works” and “every good work”, six times in three short chapters. Paul insists that grace saves apart from works, and that grace then produces people eager to do good.

cover.title: Philemon
cover.subtitle: The Letter, Its World and Your Notes
meta: Written about AD 60–62 from prison in Rome

intro.author: Paul the apostle
paras: Paul writes as “a prisoner of Christ Jesus”, with Timothy (v. 1). The letter goes to Philemon, a believer at Colossae whose house hosted the church. Philemon’s slave Onesimus had come to Paul and become a believer. Paul wrote from prison, most likely in Rome, about AD 60–62, and sent Onesimus home with Tychicus, along with Colossians (Col 4:7–9).
facts: Philemon and the church in his house at Colossae

learn.title: Thanks for Philemon
learn.text: Why Paul thanks God for Philemon’s faith and love, which had refreshed the hearts of the saints. vv.

learn.title: An appeal for Onesimus
learn.text: How Paul appeals on the basis of love, not command, for Onesimus, once unprofitable and now a brother beloved. vv.

learn.title: Charge it to me
learn.text: How Paul offers to repay any wrong himself, and trusts that Philemon will do even more than he asks. vv.

shape.label: Verses 1–7
shape.title: Greeting and thanks
shape.text: Paul greets Philemon’s household church and thanks God for his love.

shape.label: Verses 8–25
shape.title: The appeal
shape.text: Paul pleads for Onesimus, offers to pay his debt, and sends final greetings.

keyverse.text: “no longer as a servant, but more than a servant, a brother beloved, specially to me, but how much rather to thee, both in the flesh and in the Lord.”

intro.asread: Watch for the word “heart” (vv. 7, 12, 20). Paul calls Onesimus “my very heart” and asks Philemon to refresh his heart by welcoming him as a brother.

cover.title: Hebrews
cover.subtitle: The Letter, Its World and Your Notes
meta: Written about AD 60s, before the temple fell
Sent to Jewish believers, perhaps in Rome

intro.author: Unknown
paras: Hebrews never names its author. The writer knew Timothy (13:23) and heard the gospel from those who had heard the Lord (2:3), so was not one of the Twelve. Early tradition in the East credited Paul; others suggested Barnabas, Apollos or Luke, and later Priscilla. Around AD 230 Origen concluded that only God knows who wrote it.
intro.note: Most scholars today doubt Paul wrote it, since its style and approach differ from his letters. The church received it as Scripture all the same; this study leaves the author open, as Origen did.
facts: About the AD 60s, before the temple fell

learn.title: Greater than the angels
learn.text: Why the Son is God’s final word, and why He became fully human to rescue His brothers and sisters.

learn.title: Greater than Moses
learn.text: How Jesus is faithful over God’s house, and why unbelief kept Israel from entering God’s rest.

learn.title: Our great high priest
learn.text: Why Jesus, a priest forever after the order of Melchizedek, can sympathize with us and save completely.

learn.title: A better covenant
learn.text: How Christ’s once-for-all sacrifice fulfills the tabernacle, cleanses the conscience and brings the promised new covenant.

learn.title: The hall of faith
learn.text: How Abel, Abraham, Moses and many others trusted God’s promises without seeing them fulfilled in their lifetimes.

learn.title: Running the race
learn.text: How to run with endurance, looking to Jesus, receiving God’s discipline as His children and pursuing holiness.

shape.title: The Son is greater
shape.text: Greater than angels and Moses, with warnings not to drift away.

shape.title: The greater priest
shape.text: A better priesthood, covenant and sacrifice than the old system offered.

shape.title: So draw near
shape.text: Faith, endurance and love in practice, because the way is now open.

intro.turning: The turning point: “Having therefore, brethren, boldness to enter into the holy place by the blood of Jesus,” (10:19)

keyverse.text: “Let us therefore draw near with boldness unto the throne of grace, that we may receive mercy, and may find grace to help us in time of need.”

intro.asread: Watch for the word “better”. It appears thirteen times: a better hope, covenant, sacrifice, promise and country, all found in Christ.

cover.title: James
cover.subtitle: The Letter, Its World and Your Notes
meta: Sent to Jewish believers of the Dispersion

intro.author: James, the brother of Jesus (by tradition)
paras: The writer calls himself simply “a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ” (1:1). Church tradition identifies him as James the brother of Jesus, who did not believe at first (John 7:5) but saw the risen Lord (1 Cor 15:7) and became leader of the church in Jerusalem (Acts 15:13). He wrote from Jerusalem to Jewish believers scattered abroad, perhaps in the AD 40s.
intro.note: Some scholars question whether a Galilean wrote such fine Greek, and some date the letter later. This study follows the traditional view.

learn.title: Joy in trials
learn.text: Why testing produces endurance, how to ask God for wisdom, and where temptation really comes from.

learn.title: Doers of the word
learn.text: Why hearing God’s word is not enough, and what pure religion looks like in daily life.

learn.title: No favoritism
learn.text: Why showing partiality to the rich breaks the royal law to love your neighbor as yourself.

learn.title: Faith that works
learn.text: Why faith without works is dead, shown in the examples of Abraham and Rahab.

learn.title: Taming the tongue
learn.text: How a small tongue can steer a whole life, and why blessing and cursing should not mix.

learn.title: Patience and prayer
learn.text: How to wait for the Lord’s coming, and why the prayer of a righteous man is powerful.

shape.label: Chapter 1
shape.title: Trials and true religion
shape.text: Testing, wisdom, temptation and the call to do what the word says.

shape.label: Chapters 2–3
shape.title: Faith in deeds and words
shape.text: Faith shows itself in fairness, good works, careful speech and wisdom from above.

shape.label: Chapters 4–5
shape.title: Humble and patient
shape.text: Turning from worldliness and pride, warning the rich, waiting and praying.

keyverse.text: “But be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deluding your own selves.”

intro.asread: Watch how often James echoes Jesus’ Sermon on the Mount: joy in trials, mercy, doing the word, not judging, treasures that rot and a plain yes or no.

cover.title: 1 Peter
cover.subtitle: The Letter, Its World and Your Notes
meta: Sent to believers across Asia Minor

intro.author: Peter the apostle
paras: Peter names himself at the start (1:1) and calls himself a witness of the sufferings of Christ (5:1). He wrote with the help of Silvanus (5:12), with Mark beside him, from “Babylon” (5:13), almost certainly a code name for Rome. Around AD 62–64, just before Nero’s persecution, he wrote to believers scattered across five provinces of Asia Minor.
intro.note: Some scholars date the letter later and credit Peter’s followers; Silvanus’ help may explain its polished Greek. This study follows the traditional view.

learn.title: A living hope
learn.text: How God has given believers new birth and an inheritance kept in heaven, so they can rejoice in trials.

learn.title: Called to be holy
learn.text: Why redeemed people live holy lives, and how they become living stones and God’s own people.

learn.title: Sojourners doing good
learn.text: How believers honor rulers, masters, husbands and wives, following Christ’s example of patient suffering.

learn.title: Suffering for doing right
learn.text: Why it is better to suffer for doing good, and how Christ’s suffering led to victory.

learn.title: The fiery trial
learn.text: Why suffering as a Christian is no surprise, and how to entrust your soul to a faithful Creator.

learn.title: Humble shepherds and sheep
learn.text: How elders shepherd the flock, how all should be humble, and how to resist the devil.

shape.title: Who you are in Christ
shape.text: Born again to a living hope and made God’s own holy people.

shape.title: Living as sojourners
shape.text: Doing good in society, at work and at home, even when mistreated.

shape.title: Standing firm in suffering
shape.text: The fiery trial, faithful shepherds and the God of all grace.

intro.turning: The turning point: “Beloved, I beseech you as sojourners and pilgrims, to abstain from fleshly lusts, which war against the soul;” (2:11)

keyverse.text: “Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who according to his great mercy begat us again unto a living hope by the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead,”

intro.asread: Watch how suffering and glory keep appearing together (1:11; 4:13; 5:1, 10). Peter never promises escape from suffering, but he always points beyond it to glory.

cover.title: 2 Peter
cover.subtitle: The Letter, Its World and Your Notes
meta: Peter's farewell before his death in Rome

intro.author: Simon Peter the apostle
paras: The writer calls himself “Simon Peter, a servant and apostle of Jesus Christ” (1:1). He says he saw Jesus’ majesty on the holy mount (1:16–18) and knows his death is near, as the Lord showed him (1:14). Calling this his second letter (3:1), he likely writes to the readers of 1 Peter, probably from Rome, about AD 64–67, shortly before his martyrdom.
intro.note: This is the most debated authorship in the New Testament. Many scholars think a follower wrote it in Peter’s name, about AD 80–120. This study follows the traditional view.
facts: Probably Rome, near the end of Peter’s life
Believers, likely the readers of 1 Peter (3:1)

learn.title: Growing in grace
learn.text: How God’s power gives all we need for godliness, and the qualities believers should add to their faith.

learn.title: Eyewitnesses and Scripture
learn.text: Why the apostles’ message is no clever myth, and how prophecy came from men moved by the Holy Spirit.

learn.title: False teachers exposed
learn.text: How false teachers creep in, what marks them, and how God judges the wicked yet rescues the godly.

learn.title: The day of the Lord
learn.text: Why the Lord’s return is delayed by patience, not slackness, and how the day will come like a thief.

learn.title: Steadfast to the end
learn.text: How to wait in holiness and peace, read Paul’s letters wisely, and keep growing in grace.

shape.label: Chapter 1
shape.title: Grow in true knowledge
shape.text: God’s power, Christian virtues and the sure word of the apostles and prophets.

shape.label: Chapter 2
shape.title: Beware false teachers
shape.text: Their greed, immorality and sure judgment, with Old Testament examples.

shape.label: Chapter 3
shape.title: Wait for His coming
shape.text: Scoffers answered, the day of the Lord, and a call to grow.

keyverse.text: “But grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ. To him be the glory both now and for ever. Amen.”

intro.asread: Watch for the word “knowledge” and for Peter’s reminders (1:12–15; 3:1–2). True knowledge of Christ is his answer to false teaching.

cover.title: 1 John
cover.subtitle: The Letter, Its World and Your Notes
meta: Written about AD 90–95, likely in Ephesus
Sent to the churches of Asia

intro.author: John the apostle (traditionally)
paras: The letter names no author, but the writer was an eyewitness of “the Word of life” (1:1), and its language closely matches John’s Gospel. Early church writers such as Irenaeus credit it to John the apostle. Writing as an aged pastor to his “little children,” likely from Ephesus about AD 90–95, he steadies churches shaken by teachers who had left them.
intro.note: Some scholars credit the letter to a circle of John’s disciples rather than the apostle himself. This study follows the traditional view.
facts: Churches in the Roman province of Asia

learn.title: Walking in the light
learn.text: Why God is light, and how confessing our sins brings forgiveness through Jesus our Advocate.

learn.title: Keeping His commandments
learn.text: How obedience and love for a brother show that we truly know God and abide in Him.

learn.title: Not loving the world
learn.text: Why the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes and pride pass away.

learn.title: Children of God
learn.text: What it means that the Father calls us His children, and why His children do not keep sinning.

learn.title: God is love
learn.text: How God showed His love in sending His Son, and why those He loves must love one another.

learn.title: Assurance of life
learn.text: How faith overcomes the world, and how believers may know they have eternal life.

shape.label: Chapters 1–2
shape.title: God is light
shape.text: Fellowship, confession, obedience and warning against those who left.

shape.label: Chapters 3–4
shape.title: Children who love
shape.text: God’s children do right, love one another and test the spirits.

shape.label: Chapter 5
shape.title: Faith and assurance
shape.text: Faith that overcomes, the witness of God and confidence in prayer.

keyverse.text: “These things have I written unto you, that ye may know that ye have eternal life, even unto you that believe on the name of the Son of God.”

intro.asread: Watch for the word “know”. It appears over thirty times, often in the phrase “hereby we know”. John wants believers to be sure, not anxious.

cover.title: 2 John
cover.subtitle: The Letter, Its World and Your Notes
meta: Written about AD 90–95, likely in Ephesus
Sent to “the elect lady and her children”

intro.author: John the apostle (“the elder”)
paras: The writer calls himself simply “the elder” (v. 1), a title his readers clearly recognized. Its language and concerns match 1 John, and early church tradition credits John the apostle, writing near the end of his long life. Likely from Ephesus, about AD 90–95, he writes to “the elect lady and her children,” most likely a local church and its members.
intro.note: Some think “the elder” was a different John, a church leader mentioned by Papias. This study follows the traditional view.
facts: “The elect lady and her children,” likely a church

learn.title: Truth and love together
learn.text: Why walking in truth and loving one another are both part of keeping God’s commandment. vv.

learn.title: Beware of deceivers
learn.text: How to recognize teachers who deny that Jesus Christ came in the flesh, and why to remain in Christ’s teaching. vv.

learn.title: Careful hospitality
learn.text: Why believers should not welcome false teachers into their homes and so share in their evil works. vv.

shape.label: Verses 1–6
shape.title: Walk in love
shape.text: Greeting, joy over faithful children and the old command to love.

shape.label: Verses 7–13
shape.title: Guard the truth
shape.text: Warning about deceivers, a firm rule for hospitality and a closing hope.

keyverse.text: “And this is love, that we should walk after his commandments. This is the commandment, even as ye heard from the beginning, that ye should walk in it.”

intro.asread: Watch the word “truth”. It appears five times in the first four verses and binds the whole note together with love.

cover.title: 3 John
cover.subtitle: The Letter, Its World and Your Notes
meta: Written about AD 90–95, likely in Ephesus
Sent to Gaius, a faithful friend

intro.author: John the apostle (“the elder”)
paras: As in 2 John, the writer calls himself “the elder” (v. 1), and early church tradition identifies him as John the apostle. He writes a personal note to his dear friend Gaius, likely from Ephesus about AD 90–95. He hopes to visit soon and speak face to face, and the letter shows his care for the churches and the traveling missionaries.
intro.note: Some think “the elder” was a different John, a church leader mentioned by Papias. This study follows the traditional view.

learn.title: Faithful hospitality
learn.text: Why John rejoices that Gaius walks in the truth and welcomes traveling brothers, even strangers. vv.

learn.title: A proud leader
learn.text: How Diotrephes, who loved to be first, refused John and drove out those who welcomed the brothers. vv.

learn.title: Imitate what is good
learn.text: Why doing good shows we are of God, and why Demetrius is well spoken of by all. vv.

shape.label: Verses 1–8
shape.title: Praise for Gaius
shape.text: His walk in truth and his welcome for traveling missionaries.

shape.label: Verses 9–14
shape.title: Two examples
shape.text: Diotrephes to avoid, Demetrius to trust, and hope of a visit.

keyverse.text: “Beloved, imitate not that which is evil, but that which is good. He that doeth good is of God: he that doeth evil hath not seen God.”

intro.asread: Watch the word “truth” again, six times in this short note. Supporting missionaries makes believers “fellow-workers for the truth” (v. 8).

cover.title: Jude
cover.subtitle: The Letter, Its World and Your Notes
meta: By Jude, brother of James and of Jesus

intro.author: Jude, brother of James and of Jesus (by tradition)
paras: The writer calls himself “a servant of Jesus Christ, and brother of James” (v. 1). This points to James of Jerusalem, and so to Judas, one of Jesus’ brothers (Mark 6:3), who came to faith after the resurrection (Acts 1:14). He humbly calls himself a servant, not a brother of the Lord. He wrote about AD 65–80, probably to Jewish Christians.
intro.note: Some scholars think it was written later in Jude’s name, and some early churches hesitated over its use of 1 Enoch. This study follows the traditional view.

learn.title: Contend for the faith
learn.text: Why Jude changed his plan and urged believers to defend the faith delivered once for all. vv.

learn.title: Lessons from judgment
learn.text: What Israel, fallen angels, Sodom, Cain, Balaam and Korah teach about the end of ungodly teachers. vv.

learn.title: Keep yourselves in God’s love
learn.text: How to build up your faith, pray in the Spirit and show mercy to those who doubt. vv.

learn.title: The great doxology
learn.text: Why believers can rest in God, who is able to guard them from stumbling and present them with joy. vv.

shape.label: Verses 1–4
shape.title: The reason for writing
shape.text: Greeting and an urgent call to contend for the faith.

shape.label: Verses 5–16
shape.title: The danger described
shape.text: Old Testament examples and vivid pictures of the false teachers.

shape.label: Verses 17–25
shape.title: The believer’s response
shape.text: Remember, build up, pray, keep, show mercy and praise God.

intro.turning: The turning point: “But ye, beloved, remember ye the words which have been spoken before by the apostles of our Lord Jesus Christ;” (v. 17)

keyverse.text: “Now unto him that is able to guard you from stumbling, and to set you before the presence of his glory without blemish in exceeding joy,”

intro.asread: Watch for Jude’s threes: three examples of judgment (vv. 5–7), three rebels (v. 11), and three groups to help (vv. 22–23).

cover.eyebrow: A Study Of The Revelation To
cover.title: Revelation
cover.subtitle: The Book, Its World and Your Notes
meta: Sent to seven churches of Asia

intro.author: John (traditionally the apostle)
paras: The writer names himself John (1:1, 4, 9; 22:8), “your brother and partaker with you in the tribulation.” He was on Patmos “for the word of God and the testimony of Jesus” (1:9), probably in exile. Justin Martyr and Irenaeus identify him as the apostle, and Irenaeus places the vision late in Domitian’s reign, about AD 95.
intro.note: Some, ancient and modern, suggest another John, a Christian prophet, since the Greek differs from the Gospel; some date it about AD 68–69. This study follows the traditional view.
facts: Patmos, an island off the coast of Asia
Seven churches in the Roman province of Asia
About 1 hour 10 minutes, or a few sittings

learn.title: Christ among the churches
learn.text: How John sees the risen Christ in glory, walking among the lampstands and holding the keys of death.

learn.title: Seven letters
learn.text: What Christ praises and corrects in seven real churches, and His promises to those who overcome.

learn.title: The throne and the Lamb
learn.text: How heaven worships God the Creator, and why only the slain Lamb is worthy to open the scroll.

learn.title: Seals, trumpets and bowls
learn.text: How God’s judgments unfold on a rebellious world, while His people are sealed and kept.

learn.title: The fall of Babylon
learn.text: Why the great city of pride and luxury falls, and heaven rejoices at the marriage of the Lamb.

learn.title: All things new
learn.text: How God makes a new heaven and earth, dwells with His people, and wipes away every tear.

shape.label: Chapters 1–3
shape.title: Christ and His churches
shape.text: John’s vision of Christ and His messages to seven churches.

shape.label: Chapters 4–16
shape.title: The throne and the judgments
shape.text: Heaven’s worship, then seals, trumpets, signs and bowls of judgment.

shape.label: Chapters 17–22
shape.title: Victory and new creation
shape.text: Babylon falls, Christ returns, evil is judged and God dwells with His people.

intro.turning: The turning point: “Straightway I was in the Spirit: and behold, there was a throne set in heaven, and one sitting upon the throne;”

keyverse.text: “And he that sitteth on the throne said, Behold, I make all things new. And he saith, Write: for these words are faithful and true.”

intro.asread: Watch for the throne, mentioned over forty times. However wild the visions become, they keep returning
